title: A Study of the Emotional Impact of Interior Lighting Color in Rural Bed and Breakfast Space Design
research_question: The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of colored lighting within rural accommodation interiors on people's emotions and visual perceptions. Additionally, the study aims to establish an emotional dimension model to map the experimental results onto eight basic emotions, utilizing the PAD model for quantitative analysis.

participants.description: 180 volunteers recruited in Nanchang City, Jiangxi Province, China (90 experimental, 90 control). Mean age 39.2 years (SD = 20.8). Participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, were not color blind, in good general health, free of neurological, cardiovascular, autoimmune, pulmonary disorders, and were not alcohol/drug abusers.
participants.recruitment: Voluntary experimental study; participants provided written informed consent.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Six B&B rooms (6.2m L x 5.4m W x 3.7m H) with white walls/ceilings, wood floors, and windows (2m L x 1.65m H) with double sunshades/screens. Furniture included a double bed, nightstands, and wall-mounted TV. Room temperature 25°C, humidity 56%, airflow 0.15m/s. Lighting conditions included 12 scenarios combining a base white light (Warm White (RN) or Cool White (RL)) with a colored light (Blue-Red (RB), Blue-Green (GB), Blue-Yellow (YB), Red-Green (RG), Red-Yellow (RY), Green-Yellow (GY)). Light sources were LED spotlights (CCT 5300K/3000K), bedside pendant lights (CCT 6000K/6500K), and color-tunable LED strips/floor lamps.

measures.instrument: State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) questionnaire (20 items for trait, 20 for state)
Visual assessment questionnaire (9 items: visual comfort, attraction, warmth, sedative effect, peacefulness, excitement, delighted, warmth of the color, brightness)

mechanisms: Color and light are two important attributes in environmental spaces that can be used in the design and transformation of interior spaces to improve human visual perception, mood and performance.
Color in indoor environments is one of the most important factors influencing the psychology of people in the environment and guides their behavior through this psychological effect.

The brain is an electrochemical machine that is affected by all the frequencies it experiences, which are generated by light, sound and color. Information enters the amygdala, which is a key area for emotion regulation, and is then processed into the emotional body for interpretive responses.
Lighting is an artistic element that can have an impact on the human psyche.
Visual perception has an enormous impact on human mental activity.
The PAD model allows for the numerical values of emotions to be transformed into a discrete model of the six basic moods, making it easier for the reader to understand the participant's mood changes.
implementation_implications: Optimal lighting color combinations can effectively enhance customer satisfaction and positively influence customer emotions in rural accommodation spaces.
Altering lighting colors can improve perceived quality and customer satisfaction, potentially reducing costs and allowing reallocation of resources.
Lighting color theory provides reliable guidance for designers to create higher-quality and more comfortable spaces.
Warm white light followed by blue-yellow light can achieve high satisfaction among consumers in light-colored environments.
Businesses should be sensitive to lighting color choices to create desired service ambiance.
Designers and engineers can use these findings to plan indoor lighting solutions that are more appealing, comfortable, and conducive to improving physical and mental health.
The research offers objective guidance for lighting design decisions, reducing subjective decision-making.
Warm white light is an optimal choice for lobbies and corridors in rural accommodation spaces, providing warmth and comfort.
Red light should be used sparingly due to its tendency to increase unease and anxiety.
Judicious addition of cool tones can soothe moods and enhance sedative effects.

limitations: No significant effect of a specific combination of light colors on mood was found, with only blue-yellow and yellow-green light showing greater positive effects on mood than other combinations.
The short experiment duration (22 min per participant) did not realistically simulate sleep/rest over a whole night, limiting the insightfulness of emotional responses.
Participants entered the laboratory individually, not accounting for emotional responses in social settings with multiple people.
The study adhered to conventional lighting standards (warm white as primary, colored as secondary), which might limit generalizability to other design approaches.
The participant sample lacked sufficient representation of elderly individuals (over 60 years old), despite this demographic being prevalent in rural tourism.
The study primarily focused on perceptions within the cultural context of China and Asia, limiting generalizability to other countries with different color perceptions.
The study used only actual lighting fixtures and did not explore emerging technologies like virtual reality (VR) or other innovative display techniques.

paper_metadata.title: A Study of the Emotional Impact of Interior Lighting Color in Rural Bed and Breakfast Space Design
paper_metadata.crossref_title: A Study of the Emotional Impact of Interior Lighting Color in Rural Bed and Breakfast Space Design
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In architectural spaces, the ambiance created by lighting plays a significant role in influencing people’s emotions, often relying on the use of color and light. However, previous research has primarily focused on urban architectural spaces, with relatively less attention given to rural environments, especially the interior spaces of rural accommodation. The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of colored lighting within rural accommodation interiors on people’s emotions and visual perceptions. Additionally, the study aims to establish an emotional dimension model to map the experimental results onto eight basic emotions, utilizing the PAD model for quantitative analysis. To achieve this goal, the researchers recruited 90 participants and divided them into six groups, each experiencing different combinations of indoor lighting scenes with varying colors. Participants evaluated their emotions and visual perceptions. The study results indicate that the combination of cool and warm white light with colored light significantly influences the arousal level of participants but has a relatively lower impact on pleasure levels, dominance and relaxation levels. In comparing the emotions experienced after exposure to cool and warm white light followed by colored light, warm white light elicited more positive emotions. Furthermore, colored light following cool white light diminished the sense of warmth in light, while yellow–blue light enhanced visual comfort and blue–red light increased attraction. Overall, the effect of colored lighting in rural accommodation interior spaces on improving negative emotions was relatively weak. Conversely, the combination of warm white light with blue–yellow or green–yellow light had a more significant effect on enhancing visual perceptions and reducing participants’ anxiety. This research provides valuable insights and references for designing the lighting ambiance in rural accommodation interiors and lighting design, with the potential to enhance the spatial experience of rural accommodations.
